mainEntity.name: What are class attributes in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Class attributes in Java are variables declared directly inside a class body but outside any method, constructor, or block. They are also called fields or instance variables. Attributes define the STATE of an object — the data each object holds. Syntax: [access_modifier] [static] [final] dataType attributeName; Example: private String name; private int age; private double salary; Each object created from the class gets its own copy of instance attributes. Static attributes are shared across all objects of the class.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between instance attributes and static attributes in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Instance attributes belong to each individual object — every object created from the class gets its own separate copy. They are declared without the 'static' keyword: 'private String name;'. Each Car object has its own color, speed, and fuel. Static attributes belong to the class itself — all objects share a single copy. They are declared with 'static': 'private static int totalCars;'. Modifying a static attribute through one object changes it for all. Static attributes are initialized when the class is loaded; instance attributes when an object is created with 'new'.

mainEntity.name: What are the default values of Java class attributes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Java automatically assigns default values to class attributes (fields) if not explicitly initialized: byte, short, int, long → 0; float, double → 0.0; char → '\u0000' (null character); boolean → false; Object references (String, arrays, any class) → null. Note: local variables inside methods do NOT get default values — they must be explicitly initialized before use. Using an uninitialized local variable causes a compile error, while an uninitialized field safely uses its default.

mainEntity.name: What is a final attribute in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: A final attribute in Java is a field that can be assigned only ONCE — after that, its value cannot be changed. Declared with the 'final' keyword: 'private final String accountNumber;'. Instance final fields must be initialized either at declaration or inside the constructor. Static final fields are constants shared by all objects: 'public static final double PI = 3.14159;'. By convention, static final constants use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE. Final fields communicate intent: this value should never change after object creation, making objects more predictable and thread-safe.

mainEntity.name: Why should Java class attributes be declared private?

acceptedAnswer.text: Declaring attributes private enforces encapsulation — one of the four pillars of OOP. Private attributes cannot be accessed or modified directly from outside the class. This means: (1) Validation can be added in setter methods to prevent invalid states. (2) Internal implementation can change without breaking external code. (3) Read-only fields can be created by providing only a getter, no setter. (4) Debugging is easier since invalid state has only one entry point. Without private, any code anywhere can set 'student.age = -999' — an invalid state. With private + setter validation, the class acts as a guardian of its own data.

sections.title: What are Class Attributes in Java?

blocks.text: In Java, class attributes (also called fields or instance variables) are variables declared directly inside the class body — outside any method, constructor, or block. They define the state of an object — the data each object holds and carries throughout its lifetime. Every object created from a class gets its own separate copy of the class's instance attributes, holding its own unique values.

Real-world analogy: Think of a class as a form template. The blank fields on the form — Name, Age, Address, Phone — are like class attributes. When a person fills out the form (creates an object), their specific answers become the attribute values for that object. Two people filling the same form get the same attribute names, but their own unique values.

Java supports multiple types of class attributes: instance attributes (unique per object), static attributes (shared across all objects), and final attributes (constant, assigned once). Together with methods, attributes form the complete definition of what a class represents. Properly designed attributes — private, well-named, validated — are the hallmark of professional Java code.

blocks.title: 🔑 Java Class Attributes at a Glance
blocks.text: Key concepts: (1) Attribute / Field — variable declared inside class, outside methods. (2) Instance attribute — each object has its own copy; no 'static' keyword. (3) Static attribute — one shared copy for all objects; uses 'static' keyword. (4) Final attribute — value set once, never changed; uses 'final' keyword. (5) Access modifier — controls visibility: private, public, protected, default. (6) Default value — Java auto-assigns 0, false, or null if not initialized. (7) Encapsulation — keep attributes private, expose via getters/setters.

A class attribute declaration consists of an optional access modifier, optional non-access modifiers (static, final), a data type, and the attribute name. By convention, attribute names use camelCase (e.g., firstName, accountBalance). Attributes are declared at the class level — directly inside the class body, not inside any method or constructor.

items.title: Attribute Syntax
Attribute Rules
items.text:
1. Declared inside class body, outside all methods.
2. Names use camelCase — firstName, accountBalance.
3. Constants (static final) use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE — MAX_SIZE, TAX_RATE.
4. Should be private for encapsulation (best practice).
5. Java assigns default values if not explicitly initialized.
6. Multiple attributes of same type can be declared in one line (not recommended for readability).

items.title: Attribute vs Local Variable
items.text:
Attribute: declared in class body; has default value; accessible throughout all methods of the class; lives as long as the object lives.
Local variable: declared inside a method/block; NO default value (must initialize before use); accessible only within that method/block; dies when method returns.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Attribute vs Local Variable — Critical Difference
blocks.text: A common beginner mistake is declaring variables inside methods and thinking they are class attributes. Variables inside methods are local variables — they only exist while the method runs and are destroyed after. Class attributes are declared OUTSIDE all methods, directly in the class body. Another key difference: local variables have NO default value in Java — using an uninitialized local variable causes a compile error. Class attributes always have a default value (0, false, null) even if not explicitly set.

sections.title: Instance vs Static Attributes — Object-Level vs Class-Level

blocks.text: The most important distinction in class attributes is between instance attributes and static attributes. Instance attributes represent the unique state of each individual object — every object has its own copy. Static attributes belong to the class itself — there is only ONE copy shared by all objects. Confusing these two is a very common source of subtle bugs in Java programs.

rows: When class is first loaded by JVM
name, age, salary, color — unique per object
Safer — each thread's object is independent
Risky — all threads share same copy

blocks.text: The final keyword on an attribute means its value can be assigned only once — after that, any attempt to reassign it causes a compile error. Final attributes communicate a clear design intent: this value is fixed and should never change. Java uses two flavors: static final for class-level constants, and instance final for object-level immutable fields.

items.title: Static Final (Constants)
items.text: Declared as 'public static final dataType NAME = value;'. Belong to the class — one copy shared by all objects. By convention: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE names. Examples: MAX_SPEED, TAX_RATE, PI, DB_URL. Must be initialized at declaration. Accessible without creating any object: ClassName.CONSTANT_NAME. These replace magic numbers in code — 0.18 becomes TAX_RATE everywhere, making code readable and easy to update.

items.title: Instance Final (Immutable Fields)
items.text: Declared as 'private final dataType fieldName;'. Each object has its own copy, but that copy cannot change after being set. Must be initialized either at declaration or inside the constructor — not in a method. Common for: ID fields, PAN numbers, timestamps, identity values that should never change after object creation. Makes objects more predictable and thread-safe.

items.title: Final Reference Caution
items.text: When a final attribute is an object reference (e.g., final List<String> items), the REFERENCE is constant — you can't reassign 'items' to a different list. But the object it points to CAN still be mutated: items.add("new item") is allowed! To make the collection truly immutable, use Collections.unmodifiableList() or List.of() from Java 9+. Final only locks the reference, not the object state.

private final LocalDate issueDate;    // date of issue — fixed forever
public CreditCard(String cardNumber, String holderName, double creditLimit) {
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Credit limit exceeds maximum allowed");
this.cardNumber          = cardNumber;   // ✅ final — assigned in constructor
this.holderName          = holderName;   // ✅ final — assigned in constructor

blocks.title: 💡 When to Use final Attributes
blocks.text: Use 'final' for any attribute whose value should NEVER change after being set. This includes: unique identifiers (userId, orderId, PAN), timestamps (createdAt), configuration constants (MAX_RETRIES, TIMEOUT_MS), and mathematical constants (PI, E). Benefits: prevents accidental reassignment, communicates design intent to other developers, enables compiler optimizations, and improves thread safety since final fields are safely published in concurrent Java code.

Java automatically initializes class attributes (fields) to default values if you do not explicitly assign them. This is one key difference between class attributes and local variables — local variables inside methods have NO default values and MUST be initialized before use. Understanding default values prevents bugs where you assume a field is set when it has simply been left at its default.

rows: No object — be careful of NPE

blocks.title: ⚠️ null Default — The NullPointerException Trap
blocks.text: All object-type attributes (String, arrays, custom classes) default to null — meaning they point to NO object. Calling any method on a null reference throws a NullPointerException at runtime. Always initialize object attributes to a safe empty value when possible: String name = ""; List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(); int[] scores = new int[0];. Or always null-check before use: if (name != null) { ... }. In Java 14+, NPE messages explicitly tell you which variable was null, making debugging much easier.

sections.title: Access Modifiers for Attributes — Controlling Visibility

blocks.text: Access modifiers control which parts of the program can read or modify a class attribute. Choosing the correct access level for each attribute is one of the most important design decisions in Java. The golden rule: always use the most restrictive access level that still meets your needs. For class attributes, this almost always means private.

// ── Public setters with validation — controlled write access ──
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Name cannot be blank");
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid student age: " + age);
throw new IllegalArgumentException("GPA must be between 0 and " + MAX_GPA);

blocks.title: 💡 Access Modifier Decision Guide for Attributes
blocks.text: Follow this decision guide: (1) Is it a constant (static final)? → public or public static final is fine. (2) Is it an instance field? → always private. (3) Does a subclass need to directly access it? → consider protected (but prefer a protected getter instead). (4) Is it a package-internal utility field? → default (no keyword) only as a last resort. In practice, 95% of class attributes in professional Java code are private. Public instance fields are virtually never seen in production code.

sections.title: Naming Conventions & Best Practices for Attributes

blocks.text: Good attribute naming makes code self-documenting — a reader should understand what data an attribute holds just from its name, without any comments. Java has well-established naming conventions that all professional developers follow. Violating these conventions doesn't break compilation, but it makes your code look unprofessional and harder to maintain.

items.title: camelCase for Instance Attributes
items.text:
All instance and static (non-final) attributes use camelCase — start with lowercase, capitalize each new word.
Good: firstName, accountBalance, isActive, totalScore, lastLoginDate.
Bad: FirstName, first_name, FIRSTNAME, firstname.
Boolean attributes often start with 'is', 'has', or 'can': isActive, hasPermission, canEdit.

items.title: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for Constants
items.text:
All static final constants use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE — all caps with underscores between words.
Good: MAX_SIZE, TAX_RATE, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT, PI, MIN_AGE.
Bad: maxSize, Maxsize, maxsize.
This makes constants instantly recognizable in code — you immediately know it's a fixed value.

items.title: Meaningful, Specific Names
items.text:
Names should be descriptive and specific — not abbreviations or single letters (except in loops).
Good: customerName, orderDate, monthlyInterestRate, maximumRetryCount.
Bad: n, temp, x, dat, mIR, mRC.
Exception: universally understood short names like 'id', 'url', 'pi' are acceptable.
Aim for the longest name that is still clear and not redundant.

items.title: Names to Avoid
items.text:
Never use Java reserved keywords: class, int, for, if, etc.
Avoid type encoding: stringName, intAge (Hungarian notation — outdated).
Avoid redundant class name: Student.studentName → just Student.name.
Avoid confusing negatives: notActive, isNotBlocked — prefer positive forms: isActive, isBlocked.
Avoid single-character names outside loops — 'a', 'x', 'b' are meaningless as field names.

blocks.text: Encapsulation of attributes means keeping fields private and providing controlled access through public getter and setter methods. Getters allow reading a field's value; setters allow updating it — with validation. This gives the class full control over its own data: invalid values can never be assigned, and internal representation can change without affecting external code.

blocks.text: Java provides four ways to initialize class attributes. Choosing the right technique depends on whether the value is fixed, computed, or passed in at object creation time. Proper initialization prevents null surprises and ensures objects are always in a valid state from the moment they are created.

items.title: Inline Initialization (at Declaration)
items.text: Assign a value directly where the field is declared: 'private int age = 0;' or 'private String status = "ACTIVE";'. Best for: fixed default values that are the same for every object. Runs before the constructor. Simple and readable. Cannot depend on constructor parameters.

items.title: Constructor Initialization
items.text: Assign values inside the constructor body using 'this.field = value;'. Best for: values that differ per object (passed as constructor parameters) or computed from constructor arguments. Most common initialization technique. Allows validation before assignment.

items.title: Instance Initializer Block
items.text: A code block inside the class but outside any method — '{ this.createdAt = LocalDateTime.now(); }'. Runs before every constructor call. Useful when multiple constructors share common initialization logic. Less common — constructor chaining with this() is usually preferred.

items.title: Static Initializer Block
items.text: A static { ... } block that runs once when the class is first loaded by JVM. Used for complex static field initialization that can't be done in a single expression: loading config files, building lookup maps, computing large constants. Example: static { TAX_TABLE = loadTaxConfig(); }

sections.title: Common Mistakes & Pitfalls — Attribute Bugs That Fool Everyone

blocks.text: These attribute-related mistakes appear repeatedly in beginner Java code. Each one compiles successfully (or fails at runtime) in a way that surprises new developers. Study them carefully.

blocks.label: AttributeMistakes.java
lines: // ❌ MISTAKE 1: Shadowing — parameter hides field, 'this' forgotten
width  = width;   // ❌ Assigns parameter to itself — field stays 0
// ❌ MISTAKE 2: Accessing static attribute via object reference
c.count = 10;    // ❌ Misleading — looks like instance access
// Actually modifies the class-level static field
// Fix: Counter.count = 10; — use class name for static attributes
// ❌ MISTAKE 3: Assuming all variables get default values
private int fieldVar;  // ✅ gets default 0 — class attribute
int localVar;      // ❌ NO default value — local variable
// System.out.println(localVar); // COMPILE ERROR: variable not initialized
// id = "NEW"; // ❌ COMPILE ERROR: cannot assign value to final variable
// ❌ MISTAKE 5: NullPointerException from uninitialized object attribute
private String name;   // default is null
// ❌ MISTAKE 6: Modifying object via final reference
private final List<String> tags = new ArrayList<>();
tags.add(tag);  // ✅ Allowed — modifying the object, not the reference
// tags = new ArrayList<>(); // ❌ COMPILE ERROR — cannot reassign final ref

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These attribute anti-patterns are frequently flagged in code reviews in professional Java teams. Each violates fundamental OOP and clean code principles.

items.title: Public Instance Fields (Breaking Encapsulation)
items.text: Never declare instance attributes as public: 'public double balance;' means any code anywhere can set 'account.balance = -1000000;'. This makes validation impossible and future refactoring very hard. Always declare instance fields private and provide getters/setters. The only acceptable public fields are public static final constants.

items.title: Too Many Attributes (God Object)
items.text: A class with 20+ attributes is a warning sign. It's likely doing too many things at once, violating the Single Responsibility Principle. Example: a User class that stores login info, personal info, billing info, address, and preferences all in one. Split into: UserCredentials, UserProfile, BillingInfo, UserAddress, UserPreferences — each focused and manageable.

items.title: Mutable Static Fields (Uncontrolled Global State)
items.text: Static mutable fields behave like global variables — any class can modify them, causing unpredictable behavior. They make unit testing a nightmare (tests pollute each other's state). Use static fields ONLY for constants (static final) or counters with very deliberate shared semantics. Prefer passing data through constructors or method parameters.

items.title: Inconsistent Initialization (Half-Baked Objects)
items.text: Creating objects that are only partially initialized is dangerous: 'User u = new User(); u.setName("Raj"); u.setEmail("...");' — between 'new User()' and the setters, the object is in an invalid state. Prefer constructors that require all mandatory fields, so objects are always fully valid from the moment of creation.

items.title: Exposing Mutable Internal Collections Directly
items.text: Returning a direct reference to an internal list: 'public List<String> getItems() { return items; }' allows outside code to modify the list directly, bypassing all class control: 'obj.getItems().clear()'. Instead return a defensive copy or unmodifiable view: 'return Collections.unmodifiableList(items);' or 'return new ArrayList<>(items);'

items.title: Using Attributes as Temporary Variables
items.text: Instance attributes represent PERSISTENT object state — not temporary values needed only during one method call. Storing a temporary calculation result as an attribute (to avoid passing it between helper methods) pollutes the object's state and creates threading bugs. Use local variables for temporary computation; only promote to attribute if the value genuinely represents the object's persistent state.

sections.title: Java Class Attributes Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java fresher interviews, OCPJP certification exams, and campus placement tests related to class attributes and fields.

items.q: Q1. What are class attributes in Java? How are they different from local variables?
items.a: Class attributes (fields) are variables declared directly inside a class body, outside any method or constructor. They define the STATE of an object. Local variables are declared inside a method/constructor body. Key differences: (1) Scope — attributes are accessible throughout the entire class (all methods); local variables only within their declaring block. (2) Lifetime — attributes live as long as the object lives; local variables die when the method returns. (3) Default values — attributes get automatic defaults (0, false, null); local variables have NO default and must be initialized before use. (4) Memory — attributes stored in heap (with the object); local variables on stack.

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between instance attributes and static attributes?
items.a: Instance attributes: declared without 'static', belong to each individual object, every object gets its own separate copy, represent unique per-object state (name, age, balance). Created when 'new' is called. Destroyed when the object is garbage collected. Accessed via object reference: obj.attribute. Static attributes: declared with 'static', belong to the class itself, ONE copy shared by ALL objects, represent shared state (totalCount, TAX_RATE). Created when the class is first loaded by JVM. Accessed via class name: ClassName.attribute. Modifying a static attribute through any object affects what all other objects see — they all share the same copy.

items.q: Q3. What are the default values of Java class attributes?
items.a: Java automatically assigns default values to class attributes if not explicitly initialized: int/byte/short/long → 0; float/double → 0.0; char → '\u0000' (null character); boolean → false; all object references (String, arrays, any class) → null. These defaults apply ONLY to class attributes (fields), NOT to local variables inside methods. A local variable without initialization causes a compile error if you try to use it. Important caveat: object references default to null, which can cause NullPointerException if not checked before use.

items.q: Q4. What does the 'final' keyword do when applied to a class attribute?
items.a: The 'final' keyword makes an attribute assignable ONCE only. After the first assignment, any attempt to reassign it causes a compile error. Two types: (1) static final — class-level constants shared by all objects; must be initialized at declaration; by convention use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE: 'public static final double TAX_RATE = 0.18;'. (2) Instance final — per-object immutable fields; must be initialized either at declaration or in the constructor; cannot be set in a regular method. Important: 'final' on an object reference only locks the reference, not the object's state — 'final List<String> list' means you can't reassign list, but list.add() still works.

items.q: Q5. Why should class attributes be declared private? What is encapsulation?
items.a: Encapsulation means bundling data (attributes) and behavior (methods) together in a class while hiding internal state from direct outside access. Declaring attributes private enforces this — no external code can read or write the field directly. Access is only through controlled getter and setter methods. Benefits: (1) Validation — setters can reject invalid values (age < 0, negative price). (2) Flexibility — internal representation can change without breaking caller code. (3) Read-only fields — provide getter only, no setter. (4) Debugging — invalid state has only one entry point. Without private, any code can set 'student.age = -999' — an impossible state that could crash logic anywhere else in the program.

items.q: Q6. What happens if you declare two attributes with the same name — one as a field and one as a constructor parameter?
items.a: This is called parameter shadowing — the parameter name hides the field name inside the constructor body. When you write 'width = width' inside a constructor that has a parameter named 'width' and a field named 'width', you are assigning the parameter to itself — the field is never set and stays at its default (0 for int, null for String). This is a very common beginner bug. Fix: always use 'this.fieldName = paramName' inside constructors and methods when field and parameter share the same name. The 'this.' prefix explicitly refers to the instance field, not the local parameter.

items.q: Q7. Can you access a static attribute through an object reference? What is the recommended way?
items.a: Yes, Java allows accessing static attributes via object references: 'obj.staticField' compiles and works. But this is considered bad practice because it is misleading — it looks like you are accessing an instance attribute specific to 'obj', when you are actually modifying the class-level shared attribute. The recommended way is always to access static attributes via the class name: 'ClassName.staticField'. This makes it immediately clear to any reader that the attribute is static and shared. Most IDEs and linters warn against accessing static members via instance references.

items.q: Q8. What is the difference between a field with 'private final' vs 'private' in Java?
items.a: 'private' field: can be read and modified multiple times through setter methods, within the class. Represents mutable state that changes during the object's lifetime — balance, status, quantity. 'private final' field: can be assigned only once — either at declaration or in the constructor. After that, it's read-only even within the class — a setter method trying to assign it would cause a compile error. Represents immutable identity values that should never change — userId, orderId, PAN number, createdAt timestamp. Using 'final' makes intent explicit: anyone reading the code immediately knows this value is permanent. It also makes the field thread-safe by nature.

items.q: Q9. What naming conventions should Java class attributes follow?
items.a: Instance and static (non-final) attributes: camelCase — start with lowercase, capitalize each new word. Examples: firstName, accountBalance, totalStudents, isActive, lastLoginDate. Boolean attributes often start with 'is', 'has', or 'can': isActive, hasPermission, canEdit. Static final constants: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE — all uppercase, words separated by underscores. Examples: MAX_SIZE, TAX_RATE, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT, PI. Avoid: single letters (n, a, x), type prefixes (stringName, intAge), redundant class name (Student.studentName → just name), confusing negatives (isNotActive → prefer isActive). Good names make code self-documenting — the name alone should communicate what the attribute represents.

items.q: Q10. A class has a List as an instance attribute. How do you prevent external code from modifying it directly?
items.a: When a getter returns a direct reference to an internal list, external code can call clear(), add(), remove() on it, bypassing all class control. Three solutions: (1) Return an unmodifiable view: 'return Collections.unmodifiableList(items);' — external code can read but not modify; throws UnsupportedOperationException on mutation attempt. (2) Return a defensive copy: 'return new ArrayList<>(items);' — external code gets their own copy to modify; original is safe. (3) Use List.copyOf(items) — returns an unmodifiable copy (Java 10+). Best practice: return unmodifiable view for read-only access, or a defensive copy if callers need to work with a modifiable list. This is the defensive programming approach for mutable collection attributes.

sections.title: Conclusion — Class Attributes: The State of Every Java Object

blocks.text: Class attributes are the state of every Java object. Without attributes, a class is just a collection of stateless behaviors — like a calculator with no memory. Attributes give objects their identity, their data, and their ability to behave differently from one another. How you design, name, initialize, and protect attributes directly determines the quality, reliability, and maintainability of your Java code.

The difference between beginner and professional attribute design is clear: beginners use public fields, skip validation, mix up instance and static, and ignore default null values. Professional Java code uses private fields with validated getters/setters, meaningful camelCase names, static final constants with UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, final instance fields for immutable identity, and defensive methods for mutable collections.

Your next step: Java Class Methods — where you'll learn how to define the behavior of your classes, how methods work with your attributes, method overloading, return types, and how static and instance methods differ in accessing class state. ☕

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions — Java Class Attributes

items.q: What are class attributes in Java?
items.a: Class attributes (also called fields or instance variables) are variables declared directly inside the class body, outside any method or constructor. They define the STATE of an object — the data each object holds. Example: in a 'Student' class, 'private String name;' and 'private int age;' are attributes. Every Student object gets its own copy of these attributes with its own values.

items.q: What is the difference between instance attributes and static attributes in Java?
items.a: Instance attributes belong to each individual object — every object gets its own independent copy. They are declared without 'static': 'private String name;'. Static attributes belong to the class itself — all objects share one copy. They are declared with 'static': 'private static int totalStudents;'. Modifying a static attribute through any object changes it for all objects since they all share the same memory location.

items.q: What are the default values of Java class attributes?
items.a: Java automatically initializes class attributes: numeric types (int, double, etc.) → 0; boolean → false; char → '\u0000'; all object references (String, arrays, custom classes) → null. These defaults only apply to class-level attributes (fields), NOT to local variables inside methods. Local variables must be explicitly initialized before use.

items.q: What is a final attribute in Java?
items.a: A 'final' attribute can be assigned only once. After that, reassignment causes a compile error. Static final attributes are class-level constants (TAX_RATE, MAX_SIZE) — by convention named UPPER_SNAKE_CASE. Instance final attributes are immutable per-object fields (userId, createdAt) — must be initialized in the constructor. 'final' on an object reference locks the reference, not the object's content.

items.q: Why should Java class attributes be declared private?
items.a: Declaring attributes private enforces encapsulation — external code cannot read or write fields directly. Access is only through getter and setter methods, where validation can reject invalid values (negative age, null name). This prevents objects from entering impossible states, makes internal implementation changes transparent to callers, and clearly defines the class's public API. Public instance fields are considered a bad practice in professional Java code.
